method: frozen encoder + linear probe, 200 epochs, AdamW, features standardised on train stats
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop (6 GB), fp16 inference
note: top-1 is mean +/- std over 5 probe runs on identical cached features; the probe sets no seed. Treat gaps under ~0.5 pp as noise.
caveat: Ranks mean-pooled linear probing, not backbone capability. V-JEPA 2 is penalised by mean-pooling ~8192 tokens; its own classifier uses an attentive pooler.

pe_video_small.note: probe run on CPU; the GPU was occupied by an unrelated process

latency_rtx3060_laptop_batch1_fp16.method: frames pre-decoded; median of 20 runs after 3 warm-up iterations

vjepa2.note: also needs 64 frames buffered = 2.6 s of inherent stream latency at 25 fps

feature_width_control.method: PCA fit on train split only, applied to both splits; mean of 3 probe runs
feature_width_control.conclusion: PE Video still leads by ~9 pp at VideoPrism's 768-d width; the 14 pp gap is not a probe-capacity artifact.

pe_av_size_family.finding: small/base/large describe only the 4-layer temporal fusion encoder (768/1024/1792). All three share the same per-frame vision backbone, vit_pe_core_large_patch14_336, where essentially all compute goes.
pe_av_size_family.evidence: small and large extract 3570 clips in 30.8 and 31.0 minutes respectively - identical within noise.
pe_av_size_family.implication: Choosing a smaller PE-AV checkpoint buys capacity, not speed.

latency.conclusion: Difference changes sign between passes, so it is within noise (~+/-1.5%). Large's 535 ms is directly measured; small's is derived from aggregate throughput.
latency.recommendation: pe-av-small-16-frame is the better deployment pick: same latency, 5.5 GB smaller, 1.2 pp less accurate.

pe_av_size_family.base_not_benchmarked: configs/pe_video_base.json is provided but was not run; it will interpolate.
